prompt: What does the Greek word 'theatron' mean?
explanation: Theatron meant 'a place for seeing.' The fundamental theatrical situation is someone showing, others watching. Everything else — text, plot, characters, sets — is elaboration on this basic distinction between performer and audience.

prompt: Greek tragedy emerged around what date and at what festival?
options: c. 534 BCE at the City Dionysia in Athens
c. 800 BCE at the Olympic Games
c. 1 CE at the Eleusinian Mysteries
correctAnswer: c. 534 BCE at the City Dionysia in Athens
explanation: Tragedy as a literary form was born around 534 BCE in Athens, possibly as part of the dithyramb (choral songs honoring Dionysus). Aeschylus introduced a second actor; Sophocles a third. With three actors plus a chorus, complex dramatic conflict became possible.

prompt: Medieval allegorical dramas in which a soul confronted personified virtues and vices were called _________ plays.
explanation: Morality plays followed the older mystery plays (which dramatised biblical history). Their characters — Everyman, Knowledge, Death, Mercy — were personifications. Both forms revived theater through the Church after Rome's fall, and prepared the ground for the secular Tudor and Elizabethan theater.

prompt: Roman tragedy that was most influential on Renaissance writers (including Shakespeare) was written by:
explanation: Seneca's closet dramas — meant for reading rather than staging, full of declamation and gore — were enormously influential on Renaissance tragedy, including Shakespeare's Titus Andronicus. Plautus and Terence wrote comedy. Roman tragedy on the stage is mostly lost.

prompt: Match each early dramatic tradition to a description:

pairs.right: 5th-century Athens; performed at City Dionysia; chorus and three actors
Plautus and Terence; rowdy adaptations of Greek Menander
Performed by trade guilds in towns; covered biblical history

explanation: Each tradition emerged in distinctive performance contexts. Greek tragedy was civic-religious; Roman comedy commercial; medieval mystery plays guild-based. Together they form the deep history of the Western theater that revived through Renaissance commercial drama.

prompt: Which work is the founding text of dramatic theory in the Western tradition?
explanation: Aristotle's Poetics (c. 335 BCE) is the founding work of dramatic theory. Most of what survives is his analysis of tragedy — definitions, key terms (mimesis, hamartia, peripeteia, anagnorisis, catharsis), and a structural framework that dominated Western dramatic theory for two millennia.

prompt: Which of the three classical 'unities' was actually NOT in Aristotle's Poetics but added by 16th-century Italian theorists?
explanation: Aristotle argued for unity of action and mentioned unity of time in passing. Unity of place was added by 16th-century Italian theorists. The unities became orthodoxy in French neoclassical drama (Racine, Corneille); Shakespeare ignored them entirely.

prompt: Aristotle's term for the purgation of pity and fear that tragedy produces in the audience is _________.
explanation: Catharsis — purgation — is what tragedy is for in Aristotle's analysis. The release of pity and fear in safe form leaves the audience purified. Later thinkers including Nietzsche and modern critics have proposed alternative accounts, but Aristotle's framework still informs dramatic theory.

prompt: George Steiner's 1961 book The Death of Tragedy argued that:
options: Real tragedy requires belief in transcendent order; modern relativism kills it
correctAnswer: Real tragedy requires belief in transcendent order; modern relativism kills it
explanation: Steiner's argument was that genuine tragedy requires shared metaphysical ground — without it, suffering on stage becomes mere misfortune. Subsequent critics have disputed the thesis; the form has continued to be reinvented (Shakespeare, Racine, Ibsen, Miller). Whether tragedy can survive in a relativist age remains contested.

prompt: Match each Aristotelian dramatic concept to its meaning:

pairs.right: Tragic error or 'missing the mark' — not necessarily a moral failing
Reversal — the moment when fortune turns
Recognition — the moment when the protagonist realises the truth

explanation: These three concepts together describe the structural climax of Aristotelian tragedy. Oedipus Rex is the canonical case: Oedipus's investigation produces simultaneous reversal and recognition when he discovers he himself is the cause of the plague.

prompt: What's the traditional structural difference between comedy and tragedy?
options: Comedy uses verse; tragedy uses prose
Comedy ends in marriage and reconciliation; tragedy ends in death
Comedy is short; tragedy is long
Comedy is religious; tragedy is secular
correctAnswer: Comedy ends in marriage and reconciliation; tragedy ends in death
explanation: Comedy moves up; tragedy moves down. The line is blurry — many great plays are tragicomic — but this remains the classical structural distinction. What ultimately separates comedy is less plot than tone: comedy implies the world is, in some sense, OK.

prompt: Almost every modern romantic comedy is in some sense a descendant of:
options: Menander's New Comedy via Plautus and Terence
correctAnswer: Menander's New Comedy via Plautus and Terence
explanation: Stock characters (boastful soldier, clever slave, difficult father), the boy-meets-girl plot template, and the obstacle-overcome-marriage structure all descend from Menander through Plautus and Terence, then through Renaissance and Restoration comedy to Shakespeare and modern Hollywood.

prompt: Molière's 17th-century French satiric comedy attacking religious hypocrisy is _________.
explanation: Tartuffe was banned for years after its 1664 premiere because it cut too close to powerful religious authorities. Molière's other major satiric works include The Misanthrope and The Miser. Each attacks a specific human failure with brutal precision.

prompt: Bergson's theory of comedy describes laughter as arising from:
options: Something mechanical encrusted upon the living
correctAnswer: Something mechanical encrusted upon the living
explanation: Bergson's incongruity theory of comedy emphasises the gap between expectation and reality. Other major theories include superiority (Hobbes: 'sudden glory'), relief (Freud: laughter releases pent-up energy), and social bonding. None alone is sufficient; all probably operate together.

prompt: Match each comic mode to a defining example:

pairs.right: Lysistrata; political satire with named contemporaries attacked
Wycherley, Congreve; wit and sexual frankness
Volpone, The Alchemist; vices skewered with brutal precision

explanation: These three illustrate distinct comic registers. Old Comedy is closest to political theatre; Restoration comedy descends from New Comedy through Renaissance romantic comedy; Jonsonian satire makes comedy a critical instrument that exposes its targets to discomfort as much as laughter.

prompt: Around 1880-1900, theater was transformed by playwrights from which countries primarily?
explanation: Three Scandinavian and Russian playwrights — Henrik Ibsen, August Strindberg, Anton Chekhov — led the late-19th-century theatrical revolution, with George Bernard Shaw in England theorising and importing Ibsen. They insisted theater should depict ordinary life in ordinary speech with ordinary stakes.

prompt: The 'slamming door' that ended Ibsen's 1879 A Doll's House and was 'heard around Europe' marked:
options: Nora Helmer leaving her husband and children to pursue independent personhood
correctAnswer: Nora Helmer leaving her husband and children to pursue independent personhood
explanation: Nora's exit from her bourgeois home in pursuit of independence shocked audiences across Europe. A Doll's House remains the iconic example of Ibsen's modernist method — letters, secrets, old debts, and hidden infidelities surfacing to expose what respectable lives are actually built on.

prompt: Chekhov's four major plays are The Seagull, Uncle Vanya, Three Sisters, and The Cherry _________.
explanation: Chekhov insisted his plays were comedies; he fought with directors who staged them as melodramas. The difficulty of getting them right — between heartbreak and wry distance — has been a creative problem for theater ever since. All four plays are set on declining provincial estates among Russian gentry whose world is ending.

prompt: Strindberg's late plays (To Damascus, A Dream Play, The Ghost Sonata) anticipated:
explanation: Strindberg's expressionist plays — with dream logic, fragmented identities, surreal transitions — anticipate the 20th-century Theatre of the Absurd. His personal turbulence (multiple breakdowns, paranoia) feeds the work. The plays remain prophetic of much later experimental theater.

prompt: Match each modern dramatic technique to its description:

pairs.right: Characters say one thing and mean another; the unsaid is as important as the said
Imaginary boundary between stage and audience preserving the illusion
Compressed setting and naturalist depiction of class and power (Strindberg's Miss Julie)

explanation: By 1910 theater had absorbed subtext, the fourth wall, naturalistic dialogue, social criticism, and ambiguity as conventional resources. The modernist drama of the 20th century built on this inheritance; the next generation (Brecht, Beckett, Pinter) would push past realism in opposite directions.

prompt: Brecht's German term for the alienation/estrangement effect that he wanted his epic theater to produce is:
explanation: Verfremdungseffekt: the familiar should be made strange enough that the audience sees it freshly and sees how it could be different. Brecht broke the illusion deliberately — direct address, songs interrupting action, visible stage machinery, captions, actors indicating rather than inhabiting characters.

prompt: What happens in Beckett's Waiting for Godot (1953)?
options: Two men wait in a barren landscape for someone named Godot, who never comes
correctAnswer: Two men wait in a barren landscape for someone named Godot, who never comes
explanation: Audiences walked out of early productions, baffled. Within a decade the play was recognised as one of the most influential of the century. The two men consider hanging themselves, decide to leave but don't move. The next day they wait again. Godot still doesn't come.

prompt: Critic Martin _________ grouped Beckett, Ionesco, Genet, Pinter, and Albee under the term 'Theatre of the Absurd.'
explanation: Esslin's category was always loose, and the playwrights themselves often rejected it. The Absurd was a response to the Holocaust, the bomb, the Cold War, and the failures of postwar utopianism — the world looked like it had stopped making sense, and theater registered the loss.

prompt: Eugene O'Neill's autobiographical masterpiece (written 1941, performed posthumously) is:
explanation: Long Day's Journey Into Night depicts O'Neill's hard-drinking father, morphine-addicted mother, alcoholic elder brother, and tubercular younger self across one terrible day. American realist drama (O'Neill, Tennessee Williams, Arthur Miller) brought hidden family violence into the open and gave the Method tradition the roles that defined Brando's generation.

prompt: Match each major mid-20th-century playwright to a key work:

pairs.right: Mother Courage and Her Children; epic theater with Marxist politics
A Streetcar Named Desire; Southern lyrical realism
Death of a Salesman; austere socially engaged realism

explanation: These three illustrate distinct mid-century theatrical projects. Brecht wanted political action; Williams wrote lyrically of Southern fragility and violence; Miller wrote socially engaged tragedies of ordinary American lives. All three remain canonical.

prompt: How does a play differ from poetry, fiction, or essay in a basic way?
options: It is a script that becomes a play only when performed; it has at least two existences
correctAnswer: It is a script that becomes a play only when performed; it has at least two existences
explanation: A play has at least two existences: as text and as theatrical event. Hamlet on the page and Hamlet performed are related but not identical. This is why theater is fundamentally collaborative — playwright, director, actors, designers, technicians all contribute.

prompt: The role of the modern theater director became canonical primarily through:
options: Saxe-Meiningen company in 1870s Germany and Stanislavski's Moscow Art Theater (founded 1898)
correctAnswer: Saxe-Meiningen company in 1870s Germany and Stanislavski's Moscow Art Theater (founded 1898)
explanation: Until the late 19th century, plays were staged by their author, the leading actor, or the theater manager. The role of director — interpreting the script as a unified theatrical vision — was institutionalised in the late 1800s. By 1920, every major theater company had one.

prompt: Konstantin _________'s acting system, developed in early-20th-century Russia, uses 'emotional memory' to feel the character's emotions internally.
explanation: Stanislavski's system became the foundation for representational acting in modern theater and film. The American 'Method' (Lee Strasberg) intensified Stanislavski's approach. Meisner technique focused on present-moment response. Brechtian acting deliberately rejected emotional identification.

prompt: What does theater offer that film and TV cannot?
options: Liveness — performers and audience share physical space and time, and the unrepeatable nature of each performance
correctAnswer: Liveness — performers and audience share physical space and time, and the unrepeatable nature of each performance
explanation: Liveness, direct address, group experience, the foregrounding of voice and body, the text as event — these are theater's distinctive resources. None of this guarantees great theater, but the medium remains capable of effects no other medium can produce.

prompt: Match each element of theatrical design to its function:

pairs.right: Frames how the action is seen; from Greek skene to perspective scenery to minimalism
Shifts mood, isolates moments, dissolves realism — transformed by gas, then electricity
Signals period, class, character — often updates Shakespeare to other eras

explanation: The cumulative effect of design choices can transform a script. The same Three Sisters can feel claustrophobic, expansive, melancholy, or absurd depending on production design. Theatrical design is its own art alongside acting, directing, and writing.
